notes.meaning: Jesus saw the crowds following Him and went up on a hillside where He could speak clearly. He sat down, which was the customary posture Jewish rabbis took when giving formal instruction. His disciples came close to Him to learn, while the larger crowd gathered around to listen.

Jesus began to speak with solemn earnestness, opening the message now called the Sermon on the Mount. He was not explaining how to earn salvation, but showing how His followers ought to live under His royal authority. His teaching guides believers to pursue genuine goodness in their hearts and daily lives.

Jesus declares that those who are poor in spirit are truly happy. These are people who know they have no spiritual goodness of their own and must depend completely on God's grace. God welcomes them into His kingdom right now and promises them eternal joy in heaven.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition teaches that the beatitudes describe virtuous actions that, through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, merit an eternal reward in heaven.

notes.meaning: Jesus blesses those who mourn, pointing especially to people who feel deep sorrow over their sins and the brokenness of the world. This is not hopeless despair, but a godly grief that turns a person back to God for help. God comforts them with inward peace and pardon today, and will wipe away all their tears in heaven.

Jesus teaches that the meek are truly blessed. The meek are gentle and patient, choosing not to strike back or seek revenge when they are insulted or mistreated. God promises that they will enjoy His peaceful blessings in this life and ultimately inherit the new earth.

Jesus promises joy to those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, longing for God's holiness as eagerly as a starving person desires food and drink. Earthly pleasures can never satisfy the human soul, but God faithfully satisfies those who seek His goodness. He gives them spiritual strength now and will make them fully righteous in heaven.

Jesus says that merciful people are truly happy. They have tender hearts toward those who are suffering or in sin, and they actively do what they can to help and forgive. Because they show mercy to others out of gratitude for God's kindness, God will show them rich mercy in this life and on the day of judgment.

Jesus blesses the pure in heart, meaning those whose inner desires, motives, and thoughts are cleansed from deceit and unholy lusts. God looks at the condition of the heart, not just outward religious habits. Only those whose hearts are made clean can enjoy close communion with God now and see Him face to face in eternity.

Jesus teaches that peacemakers are truly blessed. These are people who do not just love quiet, but actively work to resolve conflicts, heal broken relationships, and lead others to peace. God honors them as His children because they reflect His own character as the God of peace.

Jesus declares that people who suffer persecution for doing what is right are truly happy. The world often opposes and mistreats God's people because their righteous lives expose its sinful ways. Even though they may lose their reputation, property, or safety on earth, the kingdom of heaven is their secure possession.

Jesus warns His followers that people will insult them, mistreat them, and spread malicious lies against them because they belong to Him. This blessing applies only when the accusations are untrue and suffered for Christ's sake, not when someone suffers for doing wrong. Bearing unjust reproach with patience shows that a disciple is walking in the footsteps of Jesus.

Jesus commands His disciples to rejoice and be glad when they suffer for Him, because God has prepared a great reward for them in heaven. They are not walking a lonely path, for the faithful Old Testament prophets faced the exact same mistreatment from the world. Remembering that great prophets endured these hardships helps believers stay courageous through trials.

Jesus compares His disciples to the salt of the earth. Just as salt preserves food from rotting and adds good flavor, Christians help hold back moral decay in the world through their godly lives and sound teaching. If believers lose their spiritual distinctiveness and live just like the world, they become useless and face God's judgment.

Jesus tells His followers that they are the light of the world, shining God's truth into spiritual darkness. Like a city built high on a mountain, the lives of Christians are visible to everyone around them. Since people are watching, believers must walk carefully so their conduct brings honor to the Lord.

Jesus points out that people do not light an oil lamp only to hide it under a grain basket. Instead, they place it high on a lampstand so its light can help everyone in the house. In the same way, God gives His people truth and grace so they can openly guide others, not keep their faith secret.

Jesus commands His followers to let their faith show openly through good deeds and a holy life. The goal of doing good works in public is not to seek human praise or boost personal pride. Disciples must live in such a way that others see their good actions and give praise to their Father in heaven.

Jesus makes it clear that He did not come to destroy or discard the Old Testament Scriptures. Instead, He came to fulfill the Law and the Prophets by obeying God's commands perfectly, fulfilling ancient predictions, and completing the purpose of the ceremonial rituals. God's moral law remains the permanent standard of righteousness for His people.

differ.view: Lutherans emphasize that Jesus fulfilled the law by completing its demands on behalf of sinners, offering this perfect righteousness to believers through faith.
Reformed Christians emphasize that while Christ completed the Old Testament shadows, the moral law continues as an unchanging rule of life that believers are called to obey.

notes.meaning: Jesus affirms with solemn authority that God's word will never fail or lose its binding force as long as the world lasts. A jot is the smallest Hebrew letter, and a stroke of a pen is a tiny mark that distinguishes one letter from another. Even the smallest part of God's revealed truth will remain completely secure until everything God has promised is fulfilled.

Jesus warns that no one should treat any of God's commands as unimportant or encourage other people to disobey them. Teachers who undermine God's instructions will have no honor in Christ's kingdom. But those who faithfully obey God's commands in their daily lives and teach others to do the same will be recognized as truly great.

Jesus tells His listeners that they cannot enter the kingdom of heaven unless their righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees. The religious leaders were famous for their outward rule-keeping, but they neglected inner purity, truth, and love. True righteousness is not just keeping outward appearances, but an inward transformation of the heart given by God's grace.

Jesus reminds His listeners of the ancient commandment forbidding murder, which the religious leaders applied only to the physical act of taking a life. The scribes taught that whoever committed murder would be brought before the local court for trial. By reducing God's command to an outward crime, they missed its deeper spiritual demand on the heart.

Jesus explains that the sixth commandment condemns ungodly anger and cruel speech just as surely as actual murder. Calling someone 'Raca' is an arrogant insult that mocks their mind, while calling someone a 'fool' is a hateful attack on their character. God searches the heart and will hold people accountable for harmful words and bitter tempers at the final judgment.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some Catholic expositors interpreted the judgment and the council as referring to temporal penalties in this life, reserving only hell-fire for the punishment of eternity.

notes.meaning: Jesus teaches that God rejects worship when a person refuses to make peace with someone they have wronged. If a worshiper is about to present an offering at the altar and remembers that a brother has a just complaint against them, they must stop and leave their gift. Seeking reconciliation with that person must come first, and only then will God accept their offering.
